extracted.intended_audience: general literate public / citizens interested in morals, civics, and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for writing and judging moral and political essays addressing civic virtue, private honesty, manners, and freedom of speech. Covers behavioral maxims, civic duties (taxes, honesty), rules of politeness in councils, and defenses of a free press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carping and fault-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise those critical, querulous, discontented people, that, if they wish to be respected and beloved by others and happy in themselves, they should leave off looking at the ugly leg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin uses the metaphor of a man with one handsome leg and one ugly leg: if a stranger fixates on the ugly leg, he is distrusted and avoided. The surrounding implication: undue, petty criticism alienates others and harms one's social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer virtue and immortal goods over temporal pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The happiness of rational creatures is inseparably connected with immortality; virtue is the only pledge and security of a happy immortality, so sacrificing virtue to temporal advantage is infinitely foolish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 'life of a day' insect (Hypanis) parable: finite pleasures, however long, are insignificant against eternity; the more exquisite the enjoyment, the greater the pain when it's to end. Therefore moral worth should be judged by commitment to enduring goods (virtue) rather than transient fame or pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty includes paying one’s fair share of public taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every honest man should freely and willingly pay his just proportion of necessary public expenses (taxes, duties) levied for the common benefit, advantage, and safety of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the common rationalization that cheating 'the king' is acceptable because he is rich; government revenue funds defence and public goods. Evading duties (smuggling) is morally equivalent to theft from the public purse and from poorer neighbors who will otherwise bear the burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smuggling and dealing with smugglers is a form of theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Defrauding government of its revenues by smuggling, or encouraging smugglers by buying their goods, amounts to wrongfully shifting public expense onto others and is morally condemnable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: buying tea, coffee, silks, etc. much cheaper from smugglers; when duties fall short, additional duties fall on others (even by halfpence or farthings). Compares smugglers and their abettors to pickpockets. Also cites social examples of genteel people casually requesting smuggled goods, showing the commonness and hypocrisy of the practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of postal franking is revenue theft
rubrics_metrics.description: When members of parliament or public officers frank letters not written by or on their business, it is a hurt to the revenue and an injury to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the practice of respectable people asking legislators to frank private letters; such misuse is likened to theft from the public treasure. The practice is common and reflects insensibility to justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: One cannot justify stealing from the public because the public (or sovereign) is 'rich'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no justification of a robbery that the person robbed was rich and able to bear it; the king has as much right to justice as the meanest of his subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral argument equating theft from the sovereign/public with theft from an individual; appeals to scripture ('the son that robbeth his father') and to the concept of shared public treasury for national purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect cultural difference in manners; avoid ethnocentric 'savage' judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: We call other peoples 'savages' because their manners differ from ours; if examined impartially no people are wholly rude nor wholly polite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Six Nations example to show that what we call education may undermine native skills; Indian society values different aptitudes (hunting/warfare/oratory) and measures politeness and utility differently. Advises impartial examination and respect for different conceptions of civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness rules in Indian councils: order, silence, and allowance to finish
rubrics_metrics.description: In council the old men sit foremost, warriors next, women and children behind; the speaker rises, the rest observe profound silence, and after he sits they allow five or six minutes for recollection and additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with European practices where interruptions are common. Emphasizes that interrupting another is reckoned highly indecent; this decorum produces orderly public deliberation. Note downside: their civility may inhibit clear expression of disagreement (they avoid contradicting openly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for receiving strangers: announce approach and offer hospitality without charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelling strangers should not enter a village abruptly; they halt within hearing and halloo until invited; elders receive them, place them in a strangers' house, and inhabitants freely provide victuals and repose without demanding payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes communal procedure: elders go round to inform residents, everyone contributes what they can spare; pipes and tobacco are brought before conversation begins; nothing is exacted for the entertainment. Emphasizes cultural norms of welcome and structured hospitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging other peoples' stories by one's own standards of truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: When missionaries scorn Indian origin-stories as fable, Indians reply that civility requires believing visitors' tales; one should not refuse to accept the other's customary narratives when they have shown willingness to believe ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by mutual misunderstanding about origin myths; admonishes interlocutors to recognize reciprocal expectations of civility and to avoid dismissive treatment of other cultures' traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech is a principal pillar of a free government
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech is a principal pillar of a free government: when this support is taken away, the constitution of a free society is dissolved, and tyranny is erected on its ruins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republics and limited monarchies derive strength from popular examination of magistrates' actions. Although freedom will be abused, censorship and penalties for words concentrate dangerous power in magistrates who could 'punish for words' and thereby destroy liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not entrust magistrates with power to punish words
rubrics_metrics.description: To whom dare we commit the care of repressing abuses of speech? An evil magistrate, intrusted with power to punish for words, would be armed with a weapon the most destructive and terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument warns that allowing judges to decide construction of words makes everyone vulnerable to prosecution; historical examples (Augustus, Nero) show libel/treason penalties being used to suppress dissent and manufacture guilt by innuendo or dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel laws have been abused historically to create tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws against libelling (e.g., Augustus's law) established tyranny by making words treason; judges and informers could interpret expressions, looks, even dreams, as treasonable acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical abuses: people executed for praising Brutus, for doubting Nero's musical skill, or for mourning; dreams and looks construed as evidence; the multiplication of treasons led to public terror and suppression of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit punishments for libel; avoid cruel corporal penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites statutes limiting punishments for libel (e.g., fines and short imprisonment rather than corporal punishment) as protective measures against extreme penalties used to intimidate speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References acts under Queen Mary and Elizabeth specifying fines and imprisonment and requiring proof by two witnesses; suggests legal limits can reduce abuse compared with harsher Star Chamber practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and censorship of stage and press corrupts public taste and suppresses virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment of a licenser for stage and press led to plays and writings that debased minds, promoted lewdness, sneered at religion and public spirit, and encouraged licentious satire against the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that when the licenser favors court tastes, comedy becomes double-entendre and lewd; satire is perverted from attacking vice to attacking virtue; licensure can turn stage and press into battering engines against religion, virtue, and liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should be targeted against vice, not used to debase virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire in the hands of good writers (Horace, Juvenal, Boileau) is pointed against vice; when misused, it becomes an enemy of virtue and innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques contemporary court wit who lampoon citizens and virtue; warns against art that levels its 'artillery' at civic institutions and moral character rather than redirecting critique toward genuine vice.
